facts.statement: Appalachiosaurus is a genus of tyrannosauroid theropod dinosaur that lived in eastern North America during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Appalachiosaurus ( ; "Appalachian lizard") is a genus of tyrannosauroid theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period of what is now eastern North America.

facts.statement: Appalachiosaurus was a basal member of the Eutyrannosauria clade, making it closely related to true tyrannosaurids like Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: It was a basal member of the clade Eutyrannosauria, meaning it was rather close in relation to the true tyrannosaurids such as Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Appalachiosaurus was a bipedal predator like most theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Like most theropods, it was a bipedal predator.

facts.statement: Only a juvenile skeleton of Appalachiosaurus has been found, measuring approximately 6.5 meters long and weighing 623 kilograms, suggesting adults were significantly larger.
facts.quote: Only a juvenile skeleton has been found, representing an animal approximately 6.5 m long and weighing 623 kg, which indicates an adult would have been significantly larger.

facts.statement: Fossils of Appalachiosaurus were found in the Demopolis Chalk Formation of central Alabama, dating to the middle of the Campanian age around 77 million years ago.
facts.quote: Fossils of Appalachiosaurus were found in central Alabama's Demopolis Chalk Formation. This formation dates to the middle of the Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous, around 77 million years ago.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Appalachiosaurus was discovered by Auburn University geologist David King in July 1982.
facts.quote: The type specimen was found by Auburn University geologist David King in July 1982.

facts.statement: The genus name Appalachiosaurus includes the Greek word 'sauros,' meaning 'lizard,' a common suffix in dinosaur names.
facts.quote: The generic name also includes the Greek word sauros ("lizard"), the most common suffix used in dinosaur names.

facts.statement: The genus and species of Appalachiosaurus were named in 2005 by paleontologists Thomas Carr and Thomas Williamson.
facts.quote: Both the genus and species were named in 2005 by paleontologists Thomas Carr and Thomas Williamson.

facts.statement: The only known species, A. montgomeriensis, is named after Montgomery County, Alabama.
facts.quote: There is one known species, A. montgomeriensis, which is named after Montgomery County, Alabama.

facts.statement: The known juvenile specimen of Appalachiosaurus measures approximately 6.5 meters in length and weighs 623 kilograms.
facts.quote: The juvenile specimen of Appalachiosaurus measures approximately 6.5 m long and 623 kg.

facts.statement: Open sutures between skull bones indicate that the known specimen of Appalachiosaurus was definitely a juvenile.
facts.quote: There are several open sutures between bones of the skull, indicating that the animal was definitely a juvenile.

facts.statement: Although several bones of the Appalachiosaurus specimen are crushed, it remains informative and displays unique characteristics.
facts.quote: Several of its bones are crushed, but the specimen is still informative and shows many unique characteristics.

facts.statement: Early reconstructions suggested Appalachiosaurus had long arms with three large fingers, but it is now believed to have had much shorter arms with only two fingers.
facts.quote: Early reconstructions gave it long arms with three large fingers, but they are now thought to have been much shorter and have only two fingers.

facts.statement: Two fused tail vertebrae in the Appalachiosaurus specimen may be the result of new bone growth following a minor or traumatic injury.
facts.quote: Two vertebrae of the tail were found to be fused together, which is possibly a result of new bone growth following some sort of minor or traumatic injury.

facts.statement: In the original analysis, Asian tyrannosaurs like Alioramus and Alectrosaurus, as well as Eotyrannus from England, were excluded from the classification.
facts.quote: However, Asian tyrannosaurs, like Alioramus and Alectrosaurus, were excluded, as was Eotyrannus from England.

facts.statement: The time range for Appalachiosaurus spans from the Santonian to the Maastrichtian, approximately 85.7 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Santonian to Maastrichtian (85.7 to 66 million years ago)
